title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform
summary: The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber--Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.

title: Overlap-Excluded Estimation of Participation Probabilities for Non-Probability Samples
comment: Manuscript submitted to the journal "Survey Methodology", and is currently under review. Supplementary material for this manuscript is included as ancillary material
summary: Correction of selection bias is crucial for making valid statistical inferences about a finite population using non-probability datasets. Various approaches have been proposed to correct this bias and obtain estimates of finite population quantities such as means and totals. The quasi-randomisation approaches, in particular, aim to estimate a `participation probability' for units in the non-probability dataset. These probabilities are then applied in an inverse probability weighting scheme to produce population estimates. In this paper, we propose to estimate the participation probabilities for the non-probability sample by combining the non-probability sample with an available probability sample, while excluding the overlapping units in the probability sample. When the true overlap cannot be determined, we show how the Expectation-Maximization method can be used to simultaneously estimate the overlap and the participation probabilities. We compare the performance of our approach against several alternative methods theoretically and in an empirical context, and demonstrate the efficiency gains that are possible when the overlapping probability sample is excluded.

title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning
comment: 38 pages, 25 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Amortized Bayesian experimental design (BED) enables real-time design strategies by shifting acquisition cost offline, but existing methods remain tied to the prior and task distribution they were trained on and cannot exploit additional information available at deployment. We introduce in-context amortized BED with unified knowledge encoding (IMBUE), a BED framework that admits external knowledge at deployment through a unified in-context interface. IMBUE accepts two forms of such knowledge without retraining, namely user-specified prior knowledge and observations from previous instances of the experiment. Both are encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with the accumulated observations by a shared Transformer, and a learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones. Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and remains close to the no-external baseline when it is not.

title: A Strict Upper Bound for Three-Point Weighted Selection in Planar Vector-Valued Regression
summary: We prove $F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$ for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the upper bound $15/8$. More precisely, a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ satisfies $\mathcal T_3\le(5/6-\varepsilon_0)E$ for every finite residual frame. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument that controls disappearing weights. Together with the known lower bound, this gives $13/8\le F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$. No numerical value of $\varepsilon_0$ is claimed.

title: Bias in Method-of-Moments Heritability Estimation Under Model Misspecification
summary: Method-of-Moments (MoM) based approaches for estimation of variance components --- heritability and beyond --- are central in computational genetics due to their flexibility in addressing diverse and complex models while minimizing assumptions, and ease of computation and approximation in biobank-scale data. MoM are closely related to other important methods in this area like LD-score regression. A fundamental, highly debated question relates to the bias inherent in MoM estimates of variance components when the fitted model is misspecified: since the true underlying model is unknown, the fitted model may be missing some of the components from the true model or contain superfluous ones. We offer a general mathematical formulation of this bias and investigate its properties. This leads to novel insights about the sign and the magnitude of the bias in settings of interest and allows extensions and re-interpretation of previous MoM results in the literature. One case study we pursue is in estimating gene-environment interaction variance components (GxE). We prove that when omitting environment-specific noise components (NxE), the resulting GxE estimates are strictly upward biased, even when no true interaction exists. In another case study, we consider heritability estimation, when the genetic variance components are incorrectly partitioned (such as using a single genome-wide component instead of chromosome-specific components). We derive explicit expressions for the bias in the estimate of genome-wide heritability and its dependence on LD scores within and between components. For example, if all components have the same average LD score, the misspecified heritability estimate is still unbiased.

title: Inference for Non-Probability Samples Using Error-Prone Auxiliary Information
comment: Manuscript submitted to the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A (Statistics in Society), and currently under review
summary: Non-probability samples are a potential source of rich information for making statistical inferences. However, these datasets often suffer from quality issues, in particular selection bias. The data from a non-probability sample may be combined with auxiliary information from the population or from a reference probability sample to address this bias. The auxiliary information present on these other sources is generally considered to be error-free, however this is not always the case. In this paper, we present a novel semiparametric approach to estimate the participation probabilities of units on a non-probability sample while accounting for error-prone auxiliary information in the reference data source. The approach combines a logistic regression model for the participation probabilities with a nonparametric kernel regression model for the error-prone auxiliary variables. Through a simulation study and real-world data analysis we show that our proposed approach effectively mitigates selection bias and accounts for measurement error, while estimates from methods which ignore the measurement error still exhibit some bias. The consistency of the Inverse Probability Weighted estimator produced using the participation probabilities derived from our approach is demonstrated, and a bootstrap variance approach for the estimator is described.

title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
comment: Accepted to ACM RecSys 2026 Workshop on Context-Aware Recommender Systems (CARS)
summary: User sequence modeling is widely used in recommendation and advertising. Search ranking presents an additional challenge: the current query expresses immediate intent, while a candidate product determines which parts of a user's long-term history are relevant. We present a production sequence framework for sponsored-product ranking that augments recent behavior with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbor retrieval and query-nearest-neighbor retrieval. The selected actions are encoded together with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, while candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token. Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate, and orders per impression.

title: Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares
summary: Many scientific responses take values in Riemannian manifolds, with predictors that are scalar- and/or manifold-valued. A regression analysis in such settings must provide accurate prediction with hypothesis testing for individual coefficients. Yet no current manifold-regression framework accommodates both predictor types and enables per-coefficient hypothesis tests. We propose Riemannian Ordinary Least Squares (ROLS) as a tangent space conditional-mean model, which is the ordinary least squares (OLS) analogue for Riemannian manifolds. ROLS is well-defined under an explicit injectivity condition that keeps the logarithm maps single-valued, with cut-locus conditions for branch-sensitive cases outside it. Within the local geometric setting it admits a closed-form estimator, an $O(n^{-1})$ excess prediction-error bound with explicit curvature bias, and asymptotic $t$- and Wald tests for individual coefficients. With synthetic simulations and three real-data case studies, ROLS is shown to be competitive with the state-of-the-art baselines. In addition, the per-coefficient tests agree with effects reported in literature. We envision ROLS to be a standard tool for manifold-valued regression with coefficient-level inference to support scientific discovery, which can be interpreted in the same way as Euclidean OLS. The source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyuChenPub/ROLS.

title: Modeling inter-exceedance times of extreme heat days
summary: Extreme heat days, here defined as exceedances of a local calendar-day-based 95% quantile, often occur in clusters forming multi-day heatwaves. A calendar-day based threshold allows for the detection of temperature extremes across all seasons, which may impact several economic sectors, public health and ecosystems. Previous approaches to modeling the occurrences of extreme heat events typically treat heat event duration and the time between heat events separately. We propose modeling the inter-exceedance times (IETs) between extreme heat days, allowing for a unified description within a single model. We consider several candidate distributions for the IETs of extreme heat days and find that the zero-inflated discrete Weibull (ZIDW) distribution clearly provides the best fit according to Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests. The ZIDW distribution is a flexible model for count data exhibiting excess zeros as well as over- and under-dispersion: the zero-inflation component captures the pronounced clustering of heat days, while the discrete Weibull component adequately accounts for over-dispersion. Heat days are extracted using both trend-adjusted and non-trend-adjusted thresholds. This allows the analysis of general changes in the occurrence of extreme heat days as well as changes after accounting for the general increase in temperature.

title: Choosing the basis to compare multivariate distributions: bases, copulas and optimal transport
summary: We study the choice of an orthonormal basis for comparing two probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ through their one-dimensional projections. We show that two distributions have a common copula in a given basis if and only if their optimal transport can be performed componentwise along the directions of that basis. This motivates the notion of componentwise related distributions and leads to a structural analysis of the bases in which such a representation is possible. In particular, we establish an essential uniqueness result for the corresponding orthogonal decomposition and characterize elliptical families through equality in Gelbrich's bound within location-scatter families. For general distributions, we consider the maximum, over all orthonormal bases, of the sum of the squared quadratic Wasserstein distances between the corresponding one-dimensional projections. We prove that the resulting quantity is a metric, induces the same topology as the quadratic Wasserstein distance, and lies between the Gelbrich and Wasserstein distances, with equality in the upper bound precisely for component-wise related distributions. We also derive first-order conditions for an optimal basis and establish stability and almost-sure consistency of empirical optimal bases. Simulations and examples illustrate the computational feasibility and competitive performance of the proposed procedures and suggest new applications of copulas to multivariate distributional comparisons.

title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
summary: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/ε^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $ε^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/ε^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC

title: Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control: Exact Guarantees, Limits, and Overlapping Extensions
summary:
We study group-conditional conformal risk control (CRC) for disjoint and overlapping groups under bounded monotone losses. For disjoint groups, we establish exact finite-sample conditional risk control, two-sided bounds on the group-restricted risk, and fundamental limitations arising from local support and calibration-rank granularity.
  For overlapping groups, we study two exactly valid approaches: group-restricted calibration followed by union deployment, and direct calibration of the deployed prediction-set family. We characterize the union's limiting reconciliation gap, identify conditions for its disappearance, and establish sharp lower bounds for structured losses in specified product-form models. We also demonstrate a strict size advantage for direct calibration in an ordinal model.
  Experiments show that direct calibration can reduce prediction-set size, but its efficiency depends on group structure, loss type, and shape fitting. Results on historical diabetic-retinopathy scores further illustrate these tradeoffs. Overall, local support, reconciliation slack, and threshold heterogeneity determine efficiency, with neither approach uniformly dominating.

title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks
summary: Attention and manipulation checks are widely used in survey experiments to assess respondents' attentiveness and engagement with treatment, respectively. Yet these checks are subject to measurement error, which may itself depend on treatment when checks are administered after treatment exposure. Restricting analyses to respondents who pass these checks can therefore introduce substantial bias. We propose a general statistical framework for analyzing survey experiments with pre- or post-treatment attention and manipulation checks while accounting for measurement error. We show that three separate checks suffice to identify the proportion of respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment, provided that the checks are conditionally independent among treated respondents given their true, unobserved attentiveness or manipulation status and pre-treatment covariates. Under additional mild assumptions, this result also identifies the average treatment effect among respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment. Building on these identification results, we propose an estimator that allows flexible covariate modeling and establish its asymptotic normality. Applications to framing and digital media literacy experiments demonstrate how accounting for measurement error yields treatment effect estimates that are substantively different from those obtained using conventional approaches.

title: Cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time models for competing risks, with application to the Antibody Mediated Prevention trials
summary: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials randomized participants to VRC01, a broadly neutralizing antibody, or placebo; the primary analysis estimated prevention efficacy against overall HIV-1 acquisition and against acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains. All participants were offered daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and PrEP uptake in a trial may differ substantially from uptake in other settings. It is therefore of interest to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of such acquisition under no or limited PrEP uptake. To address these questions, we extend the structural nested cumulative survival time model (SNCSTM), a causal survival model for time-varying treatments, to a cause-specific version. We show that the cause-specific SNCSTM is closely related to the Fine--Gray subdistribution hazard model, and we study identification under two frameworks. The first, based on sequential ignorability, applies when the time-varying treatment is distinct from the randomized assignment, as with oral PrEP use in AMP. The second, based on an instrumental variable, applies when the time-varying treatment represents compliance with the randomized assignment, and it accommodates unmeasured confounding between the time-varying treatment and event time. Under both frameworks, we propose consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the structural parameters. We apply the methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two AMP trials, to estimate the effects of oral PrEP use and of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains. We also estimate the counterfactual strain-specific cumulative incidence curves under no oral PrEP use and under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.

title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization
summary: Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold $η$, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if $Γ$ is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate $(η-2Γ)_+$, with an exact early exit when $η\leq 2Γ$. title: A Unified Framework for Robust Blinded Sample Size Re-estimation Based on Nuisance Parameters
summary: Blinded sample size re-estimation aims to mitigate uncertainty in nuisance parameters at the design stage while preserving the integrity of the trial. It allows the required sample size to be updated without revealing treatment assignments and thereby reduces the risk of an inappropriate sample size. Although numerous procedures have been proposed for different outcome types, a unified framework is still lacking. We therefore develop a general framework for blinded sample size re-estimation based on nuisance parameters. Within this general framework, we develop robust methods to reduce the influence of extreme observations. The proposed framework combines asymptotically linear estimators for the parameter of interest with robust Z-estimators for nuisance parameters, thereby unifying a broad class of existing procedures through different choices of estimating functions. We also propose a general principle for constructing nuisance parameters that can be estimated from blinded data. The proposed framework is supported by asymptotic theory showing that the type I error rate converges to the nominal level under regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method maintains reliable type I error control across a range of settings, including contaminated data and small pilot sample sizes. Compared with existing blinded and unblinded methods, the proposed framework is more flexible and less sensitive to outliers. A clinical trial application illustrates its practical utility.

title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
summary: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.

title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability
comment: Extended 4 November 2026 version, with supplementary material included
summary: In this article, we study heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian-process surrogates, namely Student-$t$ processes, $α$-stable processes and Gaussian processes with heavy-tailed noise. These are Gaussian scale mixtures, and the position of the mixing variable decides whether the tails can be learned from a single realization. For process-level mixtures with a free amplitude, the profile likelihood of the mixing law is data-free and is maximized by the Gaussian law, the plug-in predictive is a data-free transformation of the Gaussian-process predictive, and no estimator can be consistent for the mixing law over the model along one path. For observation-level mixtures with symmetric $α$-stable noise, the tail index is identifiable. Further, for one-dimensional inputs under fixed-domain asymptotics with $α_0<2$ and compact hyperparameter sets, a cross-fitted plug-in estimator and the Laplace marginal-likelihood estimate computed at the global posterior mode attain the efficiency bound of the model with a known regression function, also for Matérn-$5/2$ sample paths. We also characterize small-sample failures of the Laplace approximation as folds of a posterior-mode branch and give a diagnostic. Finally, in a repeated Bayesian optimization study, observation-level tails reduced regret under gross outliers, as did Student-$t$ noise, and no degradation was detected under Gaussian noise.

title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
summary: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data
comment: 42 pages, 13 figures, 16 tables. Code and synthetic data: https://github.com/Entejar/fcDPGLM
summary: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.

title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records
summary: Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.

title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
summary: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring
summary: We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.

title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
comment: 75 pages (35 main text and references, 40 supplementary material), 11 figures
summary: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.

title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
comment: 31 pages including supplements. Main text plus abstract 7605 words. Supplement 1520 words. 8 figures. 3 tables. All figures generated by latex
summary:
A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them.
  METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy.
  SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them.
  CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.

title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
summary: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
summary: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

title: ZIO: Order-Based Structure Learning for Zero-Inflated Count Data under Data Heterogeneity
summary: We propose a structure learning method for directed acyclic graph (DAG) models of zero-inflated multivariate count data. Although causal structure learning with zero-inflated Poisson models is identifiable, existing algorithms rely on local search over the DAG space, leading to poor scalability and a tendency to converge to suboptimal solutions. To address these limitations, we develop a novel order-based scoring framework that searches over variable orderings rather than directly over DAGs. Building on this framework, we further extend the method to multiple heterogeneous datasets by identifying a shared variable ordering while allowing each dataset to have its own edge set. We implement a stochastic hill climbing algorithm with a random-to-random (R2R) proposal operator to efficiently explore the ordering space. Simulation studies show competitive performance against existing methods and improved graph estimation accuracy as more heterogeneous datasets are jointly analyzed under a shared causal ordering. We apply the method to single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from a major depressive disorder study.

title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

title: Distribution-Free Symmetry Detection in Multi-Reference Alignment at Low SNR
summary: Symmetry can reveal the structure of a signal, but detecting it becomes difficult when observations are noisy and randomly transformed. We study how to infer symmetry directly from multi-reference alignment data with additive isotropic Gaussian noise of known variance, without aligning the observations or knowing how the transformations were sampled. For cyclic symmetry, we identify a simple statistical signature that yields tests with exact finite-sample error guarantees. We demonstrate their performance even at very low signal-to-noise ratios. Dihedral symmetry presents a deeper challenge: we show that, for some signals, invariant moments below a sharp order threshold cannot distinguish reflectional from purely rotational symmetry. For generic signals, however, this distinction emerges much earlier. We use these insights to develop tests for dihedral symmetry with asymptotic error control under explicit nondegeneracy conditions. Together, the results clarify what we can learn about symmetry from noisy, unaligned data and suggest a path toward symmetry inference in cryo-EM.

summary: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

title: Conformal Prediction for Multi-Step Forecasting: Conditional Coverage and Sharp Score Calibration Rates
summary: Uncertainty quantification in prediction is a central problem in statistics and machine learning. Conformal prediction provides a flexible approach to constructing prediction sets with valid marginal coverage under exchangeability. In this paper, we investigate conformal prediction for both one-step and multi-step forecasting from a single stationary time series, addressing temporal dependence and the additional challenges of joint prediction across multiple horizons. We propose a kernel-based framework, called Time series Residual Analysis for Calibration with Kernels (TRACK), for estimating conditional quantiles of residual scores and constructing prediction sets from rolling-window forecasters. The framework accommodates heterogeneous uncertainty across horizons and accounts for dependence induced by rolling estimation, while allowing predictor memory and forecast horizons to grow with the sample size. Our finite-sample bounds quantify how temporal dependence and overlapping score windows affect calibration and coverage. We further derive bounds for conditional quantile estimation and pointwise conditional coverage discrepancy. The guarantees extend to more general predictors that admit an accurate rolling-window approximation. We also derive matching minimax bounds over classes of known score maps, clarifying how overlapping score windows affect calibration accuracy. Experimental results from simulations and applications to wind energy generation and bike sharing demand show that our methods improve regional conditional coverage while maintaining competitive interval widths.

title: Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations

summary: Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. No method dominates. Graph-based borrowing improves on covariate balancing in several settings, but a selective-coverage design favors covariate balancing. summary: The idea of testing whether the past of one signal improves the prediction of another can be traced back to Wiener. It was Granger who formalized the concept. Granger causality has become one of the most widely used tools to infer directed interactions between the components of a system. The name however can be misleading: it detects predictive relations among the measured signals, not causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them. This article starts by reviewing recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis. It then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models, and asks under which conditions that structure can be read causally.

We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

summary: We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial field through a single penalised objective. The method is motivated by applications in which the spatial effect is not a nuisance to be removed but a quantity of interest that must be recovered alongside the covariates. In insurance, for example, practitioners need both flexible nonlinear covariate effects and an interpretable geographic risk surface that can be reported on its own. Existing approaches often involve trade-offs, offering flexible covariate modelling but no explicit spatial field, rigorous spatial inference with a fixed additive covariate structure, or a combination of both at computational costs that limit practicality for large datasets. SAMBoost addresses these goals within the boosting loop, and the underlying mesh produces a sparse precision structure whose cost is largely independent of sample size. On simulations and on an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves on the predictive accuracy of joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches. summary: We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. summary: Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. We model uncertainty about this function using a Bayesian framing which allows for the use of experiments from separate studies, grounding an adaptive causal discovery principle on historical experimental data. We demonstrate its usefulness in partial identification of causal effects, and discuss how the promising results can motivate new principles for general causal discovery.

summary: Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. title: Causal Outcome Learning with Noisy Proxies
comment: An R implementation of SCOUT is available at https://github.com/ericstrobl/SCOUT
summary: Modern observational biomedical datasets contain increasingly extensive baseline and outcome measurements, yet detecting a clinically meaningful treatment effect remains difficult because investigators must identify an outcome that captures treatment response while adjusting for confounding distributed across numerous noisy baseline variables. summary:

The question of building adaptive procedures to both $β$ and $m$ is investigated, and we show that a polynomial loss for adaptation must be paid in general. We instantiate our results for Matérn Gaussian process and deep ReLU network priors. Numerical experiments for existing and new robust algorithms are provided, illustrating the practical applicability of our results.

title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data

summary: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.

summary: In this paper, we incorporate the Dirichlet--multinomial distribution into the generalized linear latent variable model (GLLVM) framework to accommodate high-dimensional, overdispersed compositional count data and capture complex covariation among taxa with a low-rank structure. Such data are compositional and often highly sparse for various reasons, posing challenges for statistical analysis. Conventional zero-replacement approaches ignore the underlying causes of zeros, further complicating the analysis. Since the marginal likelihood has no closed-form expression, we develop a variational approximation (VA) approach for efficient parameter estimation. Simulation studies and applications to two microbiome datasets are presented to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.

summary: Subset size determines the balance between robustness and efficiency in minimum covariance determinant estimation. Conventional choices fix this balance before the extent and structure of contamination are known. Reweighting does not remove the influence of the initial subset size. We propose a data-adaptive rule based on ordered squared Mahalanobis distances. It selects the first window maximum, with window width proportional to the sample size. For smooth elliptical distributions with small one-point contamination, we characterize the first population window maximum. A fast depth-based implementation reuses one ordering across candidate sizes. Simulations under Gaussian and heavy-tailed sampling show gains over fixed subset sizes, most consistently for scatter estimation.
